en: The Meaning of the Peaceful Practices in the Lotus Sutra, Expounded by the Great Dhyāna Master Huisi of Nanyue. Regarding the preaching of the Lotus Sutra:
it is the Mahayana of sudden awakening; one awakens to it spontaneously without a teacher and swiftly attains the Buddha-way. First.
This Dharma-door is difficult for all the world to believe.
Any newly initiated bodhisattva who wishes to seek the Mahāyāna,
to surpass all other bodhisattvas, and to swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood [should practice this].
One must maintain the precepts, practice patience, and exert oneself in diligence to cultivate meditative concentration.
With single-minded devotion, one should diligently study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
One should contemplate all sentient beings with the thought that they are identical to the Buddha.
With palms joined, one should prostrate as if showing reverence to the World-Honored One;
furthermore, one should regard all sentient beings with the thought that they are great Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends.
Thus, one should seek the Buddha-way with courageous and diligent effort.
As for the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s difficult and arduous practices:
in the past, during the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī,
he was known as the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana.
Having heard the Lotus Sutra, they will diligently seek Buddhahood and attain the supernatural powers of a Buddha within a single lifetime,
just like King Wonderful Adornment of the past.
Having abdicated the royal throne to his younger brother,
the king, along with his ministers, queen, crown prince, and all internal and external retinues,
went forth into homelessness within the Dharma of King Meghasvararāja.
Reciting the Lotus Sūtra and single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way,
after eighty-four thousand years, he will in one lifetime fully possess the supernormal powers of all Buddhas and receive the prediction of his future Buddhahood.
At that time, the lifespan of the people will be very long, reaching eighty-nine thousand years.
It is equivalent to eighty-four hundred years in Jambudvīpa today;
it is equivalent to eighty-four years in the other three continents.
At present, the lifespan of humans is short.
In this evil age, the kalpa-turbidity brings much suffering and affliction;
therefore, it is easy to attain the Way here.
One who contemplates all sentient beings with the thought that they are like the Buddha— [attains it].

As it is taught in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta," those who diligently practice meditative concentration should do so as described at the beginning of the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are fully endowed with the treasury of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya-garbha) and are in no way different from the Buddha.
As it is said in the *Buddhagotra-sūtra* (Fo zang jing):
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are profoundly serene and pure.
Sentient beings, however, are hindered by the delusions of a distracted mind;
their six sense faculties are darkened and turbid, so that the Dharma-body does not manifest,
just as the reflection of a face does not appear in a mirror covered with dust and grime.
Therefore, practitioners should diligently cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
By purifying the stains of the afflictive obstructions, the *dharmakāya* manifests.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
The Dharma Master’s naturally born, pure eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so.
When practicing dhyāna, he does not perceive phenomena as being either permanent or impermanent.
As it is said in the *Sukhāvyūha* (The Land of Bliss):
"The bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being neither permanently abiding nor subject to arising and ceasing."
This is called the place frequented by the wise.
Those who seek the unsurpassed path and study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* shall realize the nectar of immortality with their body and mind; it is the gateway to the pure and wondrous Dharma.
Maintaining the precepts and practicing patience, cultivating all meditative concentrations,
and attaining the samādhis of all Buddhas; with the nature of the six sense faculties purified,
the Bodhisattva studies the Lotus Sūtra and fulfills two kinds of practice.
First is practice without signs; second is practice with signs and without signs.
Through the four kinds of peace and bliss, one contemplates the six sense faculties within profound and wondrous meditative concentration: all phenomena are primordially pure.
The nature of sentient beings is stainless; it is without origin and without purity.
Without practicing the conduct of remedies, one naturally transcends all sages;
awakened spontaneously without a teacher, one does not proceed through gradual stages.
His understanding is identical to that of all Buddhas; his wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still, and his nature is supremely sublime.

He possesses the six supernormal powers and practices pure, peaceful, and blissful conduct, never wandering onto the paths of the two vehicles, but proceeding instead upon the Eightfold Path of the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva’s great compassion, Fully endowed with the practice of the One Vehicle,
The profound Tathāgatagarbha, Ultimately free from decay and aging—
This is called Mahāyāna, The Eightfold Noble Path of the Tathāgata.
Sentient beings have no five desires, nor do they sever afflictions;
this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the Great Mahāyāna.
If sentient beings practice according to its teaching, they will naturally attain the Buddha-way.
What is called the One Vehicle? It means that all sentient beings, by virtue of the Tathāgatagarbha, are ultimately and eternally peaceful and blissful, just like the lion’s roar;
this is the Buddha’s teaching between [the states of] nirvāṇa.
"World-Honored One, regarding the meaning of true nature, is it one or is it not one?
The Buddha answered the Lion’s Roar: "It is both one and not one;
It is neither non-one nor not non-one. How can it be called 'one'?"
It is said that all sentient beings are of the One Vehicle;
why then is it called "not one"? Because it is not a numerical phenomenon, why is it "not non-one"? [For] number and non-number are both absent.
Because all are unattainable, this is called the meaning of "sentient beings.
[The questioner] asked:
"Why is it named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?"
What, furthermore, is meant by the meaning of the One Vehicle?
What, furthermore, is meant by the Tathāgatagarbha? And what is named Mahāyāna?
Furthermore, why is it called the Great Mahāyāna?
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the word "mahā" means great,
and "yāna" means vehicle.
It is also called "reaching the other shore.
How can there be yet another Great Mahāyāna?
And how is it further named the "meaning of sentient beings"?
The answer is:
"Sublime" refers to the sublimity of sentient beings;
"dharmas" refers precisely to the dharmas of sentient beings.
The term "lotus" is a metaphorical expression.
For example, among the flowers of the world, whether aquatic or terrestrial,
there are those that are withered, deceptive, and unreal.
Those that are real are very few.
If it were a lotus, it would not be like this;
for among all lotuses, there are none that are "mad" flowers.
Where there is a flower, there is fruit.
While the fruits produced by other flowers are manifest and easy to perceive,
the fruits produced by the lotus flower are hidden and difficult to see.
The "wild flowers" are a metaphor for the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The other flowers, which bear fruit and are manifest and easy to recognize,
refer to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
This also represents the distinctions in the superiority and inferiority of the sequential paths practiced by bodhisattvas of dull faculties;
their severance of the accumulation of afflictions is likewise termed "manifest and easy to understand.
The bodhisattvas of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are not like this.
They do not practice in a gradual sequence,
nor do they sever their afflictions;
yet, by realizing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they ultimately attain the path to Buddhahood.
If one practices the path of the Lotus Sutra, one does not travel by the way of the two vehicles.
A question is asked:
"Other flowers produce fruit one by one; how is it that a single flower produces a single fruit?"
A single lotus flower produces many fruits.
Is it not the One Vehicle that there is one flower and one fruit?
Is it not the sequential progression that a single flower produces many fruits?
The answer is:
Among all flowers of the waters and the land,
those that produce a single fruit from a single flower are very few.
Those who fall away and fail to achieve success are exceedingly numerous;
it may be said that they are like wild blossoms that bear no fruit.
Only one flower produces one fruit.
If one generates the mind of a śrāvaka, there is the fruit of a śrāvaka;
if one generates the mind of a pratyekabuddha, there is the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
These cannot be called the bodhisattva or the buddha fruit.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva of dull faculties cultivates the practices of remediation and enters the path in successive stages, ascending to the first bhūmi,
at that time it cannot yet be called the Dharmameghā Bhūmi.
The cultivation and realization of each stage occur sequentially rather than simultaneously;
therefore, it is not said that a single flower produces many fruits.
For the Bodhisattva of the Lotus Sūtra, it is not like this.
With a single mind and a single practice, all fruits are universally prepared;
they are fully possessed at once rather than entered through a gradual sequence.
It is also like a lotus flower, wherein a single blossom produces many fruits.
When these are all simultaneously perfected,
this is called the meaning of the One Vehicle for sentient beings.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
There may be bodhisattvas who skillfully know how to proceed from one stage to the next.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Siyi jing) states:
"There may be bodhisattvas who do not proceed from one stage to the next."
"Proceeding from one stage to another" refers to the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of dull faculties who train sequentially within the path of skillful means.
Those who do not proceed from one stage to another are bodhisattvas of sharp faculties;
they are upright and abandon skillful means, not practicing the gradual stages of cultivation.
If one realizes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, all fruits will be fully perfected.
It is asked:
What is meant by "the excellence of sentient beings"?
What, furthermore, is called the dharma of sentient beings?
The answer is:
the excellence of sentient beings.
The bodies of all persons possess six kinds of sublime characteristics,
because the nature of the six sovereign kings is pure.
As for these six kinds of characteristics:
These are the six sense faculties.
There are those who seek the Way, uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, recite and practice it,
and contemplate the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, knowing that the eighteen realms have no inherent nature.
They attain profound meditative concentration and are endowed with the four kinds of sublime and peaceful conduct.
They attain the six supernormal powers and the pure, natural eye born of their parents.
Upon attaining this eye, they skillfully know the spheres of all Buddhas.
He also knows the karmic conditions of all sentient beings, as well as the retributions of their form and mind;
he knows in a single thought-moment their birth and death, their emergence and disappearance, their high and low status, and their beauty or ugliness.

Within this divine power of the eye, he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, the three types of clear knowledge, the eight liberations, and all supernatural powers—all of which are simultaneously perfected within the divine power of the eye.
Is this not the wondrous eye of sentient beings?
The wondrous eye of sentient beings is precisely the Buddha-eye.
Why is it called "various"?
There are two:
first, the lineage of ordinary beings;
second, the lineage of noble ones.
Generally, those who sow [the seeds of affliction] cannot awaken to this:
that because they see forms with their eyes, they give rise to craving and attachment.
Craving itself is ignorance acting as craving;
the performance of karma is called "formative action" (saṃskāra);
and according to that karma, one receives retribution.
Because they travel throughout the various realms of gods and humans across the six paths of existence,
they are called "conduct" (*caryā*).
Because they continue in an uninterrupted succession, they are termed "seeds" (*bīja*).
This is called the seed of the ordinary person.
As for the seed of the noble ones,
it is that which, through a spiritual friend, is well awakened to and thoroughly understood.
When seeing forms with the eye,
one should reflect thus:
"Who is it that sees these forms now?"
Is it the eye-faculty that sees?
Is it the eye-consciousness that sees?
Or is it space and light that see?
Is it that form itself sees by means of the mental consciousness?
If the mental consciousness were to see form, then a blind person should also see form.
If form itself were to see, the same would apply.
If it were empty space that sees clearly,
then empty space would have no mind;
furthermore, lacking the faculty of sensory contact, it would be unable to see forms.
If visual consciousness were able to see,
then consciousness would have no intrinsic nature and would depend upon a multitude of conditions;
yet these conditions are empty in nature, possessing neither conjunction nor disjunction.
Examining each one with careful attention,
one seeks the eye but does not find it;
nor is there even the name "eye."
If the eye were able to see,
then even those who are blind from birth should see forms. Why is this?
Because the faculties are not destroyed.
When observing in this way,
there is no eye, no forms, and no seer.
Furthermore, there is nothing that is not seen.
The bodies of men, women, and others originally arise from a single moment of ignorance—the failure to understand—which gives rise to this deluded mind of discursive thought.
This deluded mind of discursive thought, in turn, produces these various forms.
It is like space; the body is like a dream, like a shadow, like a flame, and like a magical creation.
It is also like a flower in the sky, unobtainable upon seeking.
Being neither subject to annihilation nor permanence, when the eye encounters forms, there is no craving or attachment.
Why is this? Space cannot harbor craving;
space does not sever ignorance, nor does it give rise to wisdom.
At that time, afflictions are themselves bodhi;
ignorance conditioned by formations is itself nirvana;
and so it is, even unto old age and death.
If dharmas are without arising, there is no aging or death.
Because they do not cling to any dharmas, they are called the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Whether they be ordinary or noble lineages, they are neither one nor two.
Ignorance and non-ignorance are likewise thus;
therefore, it is called the subtle characteristic of the eye-element.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise thus.
Regarding the purity of the nature of the six sovereign kings:
the first is the eye king.
Because one sees forms with the eye, greed and attachment arise.
Craving is none other than ignorance;
all afflictions belong to craving.
This craving and ignorance cannot be restrained;
they are sovereign like a king.
As for those whose nature is pure:
As explained above in the section on the contemplation of the eye,
one uses adamantine wisdom to realize the nature of craving;
this is precisely the absence of ignorance and the absence of old age and death.
This Vajra-wisdom possesses the greatest power;
it is named the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
It is like a valiant general who is able to subdue enemies.
It can cause the worlds of the four directions to become pure.
This vajra-wisdom is likewise:
it is able to contemplate that craving, ignorance, and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are themselves the bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the noble practice (*āryacaryā*).
Ignorance and craving are themselves the vajra wisdom of bodhi.
The nature of the Sovereign King of the Eye is primordially pure and cannot be defiled.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
The eyes born of one's parents are pure and constant;
the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras state that the nature of the six sovereign kings is pure.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said:
"One should know that the six characteristics of the human body are wondrous."
The human body is the very body of sentient beings;
the body of sentient beings is the body of the Tathāgata.
This is because the bodies of sentient beings are one with the Dharma-body, which is immutable and unchanging.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the section on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), states:
"Its nature has been quiescent from the beginning, without arising or ceasing;
from the very outset it is empty, forever free from all afflictions."
Having realized that all phenomena are thus,
one transcends and attains the path of Buddhahood.
If ordinary people can awaken to these real dharmas of the aggregates, [they shall likewise attain liberation].
As in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha:
"What is the meaning of that which is called 'syllables' (*akṣara*)?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "There are fourteen sounds which are called the meaning of syllables (*akṣara*).
What is called a 'syllable' is named bodhi;
because it is eternal, it does not flow."
That which does not flow is precisely the inexhaustible.
Now, that which is inexhaustible is the Tathāgata’s adamantine body.
It is asked:
What is meant by "because it is permanent, it does not flow"?
The answer is:
because the eye is permanent, it is called "not flowing."
What is meant by "eternal"?
It is eternal because it is unarisen. Question:
What is non-arising?
The answer is:
because the eye does not arise.
Why is this? When the eye sees forms and one contemplates the origin of the eye, seeking for the eye, it cannot be found;
thus there is neither consciousness nor form.
Because the eye-element is empty, it is neither subject to annihilation nor eternal;
nor is it the middle way.
The eye-element is itself the dharma-realm of all buddhas.
One realizes that this eye has no beginning and no place of origin, nor even a state of being without beginning;
it is like space, not encompassed by the three periods of time,
as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita:
"Good son, empty dharmas neither come nor go;
empty dharmas are themselves the Buddha."
The dharma of non-arising neither comes nor goes;
the dharma of non-arising is itself the Buddha.
The dharma of non-extinction neither comes nor goes.
The dharma that is non-extinguished is itself the Buddha.
Therefore, one should know that because the eye-element is empty,
that which is empty is eternal.
Because the eye is empty and eternal,
the eye is itself the Buddha-eye, free from craving and attachment.
That which craves is itself the flow.
Flow is itself the arising of the eye of birth;
when there is no craving, there is no flow.
If there is no flow, then there is no arising of the eye of birth.
Because it is unarisen, there is neither coming nor going.
Non-arising is itself the Buddha-eye.
Since there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation.
Cessation is called exhaustion.
Since the eye has no cessation,
one should know that it has no exhaustion.
Since the eye is not exhausted,
it neither comes nor goes,
nor does it have a place of abiding.
The inexhaustibility of the eye is itself the Buddha.
By means of this vajra-like wisdom, the bodhisattva knows the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Because the suchness of all dharmas—such as the unarisen and inexhaustible eye—is itself the Buddha, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because his adamantine body awakens to all phenomena as they truly are, he is called the Tathāgata;
it is not that the Tathāgata possesses only a golden-colored body.
Because he has attained knowledge of reality as it is, he is designated as the Tathāgata.
Because he has attained the knowledge of the eye and forms as they truly are,
and the knowledge of the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena as they truly are, he is called the Tathāgata.
His vajra-body understands the nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) according to reality.
It is as explained according to the nature of phenomena:
as it is said that there is no arising,
so it is said that there is no ceasing.
The Buddha comes in this manner and never departs again;
because he rides upon the path of suchness, he is called the Tathāgata.

Question: In which sutra does the Buddha state that the eye and other dharmas are called "Tathāgata" because they are suchness (tathatā)? Answer: [The Buddha states this] in the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*.
In the Mahā-vīrya-prahāṇa-sūtra,
the Buddha asked Aṅgulimāla:
"What is called 'the single training'?"
Aṅgulimāla replied to the Buddha:
"The term 'one' refers to the learner;
the term 'vehicle' (yāna) signifies the meaning of being able to cross over."
It is also called "carrying across.
In Aṅgulimāla’s tenfold response to the Buddha, one response consists of two types of feet,
making twenty responses in total.
Now, to speak briefly, from the fifth answer up to the sixth answer given by Aṅgulimāla,
the meaning of the Tathāgata regarding the eye and so forth is explained in general through these four types of answers in those two locations.
What are the five that are so named?
They are the aforementioned five faculties;
this refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
This is not the meaning of the Tathāgata.
What, then, is the meaning of the Tathāgata?
It is that which is called the eye-faculty.
One constantly and clearly perceives all Tathāgatas with certainty,
and fulfills their cultivation without deficiency.
That which is called the ear-faculty constantly, definitively,
and clearly hears all Tathāgatas.
The cultivation that is complete and without decrease,
namely that nose-faculty,
is ever-present in all Tathāgatas.
One clearly and definitively smells;
one practices fully and without deficiency—
that which is called the tongue-faculty.
Regarding all Tathāgatas, one constantly and with certainty clearly tastes [the Dharma],
possessing complete and undiminished cultivation.
That which is called the body-faculty (kāyendriya) is,
with respect to all Tathāgatas, eternally,
definitively, and clearly characterized by contact.
He is fully endowed with unimpaired cultivation;
that is to say, his mental faculty is ever-present toward all Tathāgatas.
With decisive and clear discernment,
one fulfills the practice without deficiency. What are these six?
What are called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle;
they are not the meaning of the Tathāgata.
That which is called the sense-base of the eye is, for all Tathāgatas,
the gateway of constant and clear vision.
The cultivation of the ear-base is fully perfected and without decrease;
it is eternal throughout all Tathāgatas.
Clearly hearing the arrival at the gateway,
one practices fully and without deficiency;
that is to say, the sense base of the nose.
Regarding all Tathāgatas as eternal,
clearly perceiving the gateway of their arrival,
one fully possesses and practices them without diminution.
That which is called the sense-base of the tongue is, for all Tathāgatas,
eternally the gate of clear tasting.
The cultivation that is complete and without decrease,
namely the sense-base of the body,
is constant in all Tathāgatas.
The clear contact enters through the gateway;
it is the complete and undiminished cultivation of what is called the sense-base of the mind.
Regarding all Tathāgatas as eternal,
with a clear and decisive consciousness,
one enters the gateway through pure faith.
Because they possess complete and undiminished cultivation,
even those newly trained bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [should practice this].
One should skillfully contemplate the origin of the eye,
which is ultimately without arising or ceasing;
so too for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Its nature, from the very beginning,
is neither interrupted nor eternal;
it is quiescent, without arising or ceasing.
The nature of form is neither empty nor provisional;
it neither perishes nor arises.
Its nature is pure and equal to suchness.
Ultimately there is neither arising nor ceasing;
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects have been empty from the very beginning.
Neither light nor darkness;
quiescent, without arising or ceasing. Since the sense faculties and their objects are both empty and still, [the mind is likewise so].
The six consciousnesses are thus non-arising;
the three, the six, and their suchness-nature—
within the eighteen realms, there are no names.
Sentient beings and the Tathāgata share one and the same Dharma-body,
pure and wondrous beyond compare.
It is titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Therefore, in the Great Assembly,
the Buddha addressed King Viśvaghosa:
Your name is Viśuddhasvara.
You should purify your own realm;
your own realm, the eye-realm, is empty.
This is the purity of ethical discipline,
because the sphere of the eye is empty and quiescent;
this is the purity of the Buddha-field.
The nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body,
and mind is ultimately empty and quiescent;
this is what is called the Tathāgatas.
On the Meaning of Cultivating the Pure Land. Question:
What is meant by "peaceful and blissful conduct" (sukha-vihāra)?
What further are called the four kinds of peace and happiness?
What further are called the two kinds of practice?
The first is the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).
The second is practice with signs.
The answer is:
because the mind does not waver amidst all phenomena, it is called "tranquility" (āśvāsa).
Because there is no aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) among all phenomena, it is called "bliss.
Because it benefits both oneself and others, it is called "practice.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of peaceful and blissful practices (*caturvidha-sukha-caryā*).
The first is named the Practice of Peaceful Conduct Free from Attachment through Right Wisdom;
the second is named the Practice of Peaceful Conduct Free from Disparagement or Praise,
also called the Practice of Peaceful Conduct that Turns All Śrāvakas toward the Attainment of Buddha-Wisdom.
The third is called the "Peaceful Practice of Non-affliction and Equanimity," also known as the "Peaceful Practice of Reverencing Spiritual Friends.
The fourth is called the "Peaceful Practice of Compassionately Guiding Others."
It is also called the practice of peaceful dwelling that fully accomplishes the Buddha-way, supernatural powers, wisdom, and nirvana within a dream.
Furthermore, regarding the two types of practitioners,
for what reason is it called "practice without marks" (animitta-caryā)?
The practice of signlessness is itself the practice of peace and bliss among all dharmas.
Because the characteristics of the mind are quiescent and ultimately non-arising,
it is called "practice of signlessness.
It is constantly present within all profound and wondrous meditative concentrations.
Because the mind is constantly concentrated during all modes of conduct— walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, drinking, and speaking—
the various other meditative concentrations proceed through the three realms in succession.
From the stage of the desire realm,
the stage of access concentration, and the stage of the first dhyāna.
The stage of the second dhyāna,
the stage of the third dhyāna,
and the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
The stage of the sphere of infinite space,
the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
The stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
thus, there are eleven distinct stages in this sequential order,
differentiated by the two paths of existence and non-existence.
This is the noble practice of the *Abhidharma-saṃyukta-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
In the "Practice of Peaceful Abiding," profound and wondrous meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is not like this. Why is that?
Not relying on the desire realm,
not dwelling in the form or formless realms,
they practice such meditative concentration.
This bodhisattva practices universally;
because he ultimately has no mental activity,
it is called "practice without signs."
Furthermore, there is practice with signs.
This refers to the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra with a distracted mind while practicing with diligence, as described in the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation."
Such persons do not cultivate meditative concentration nor enter into samādhi;
whether sitting, standing, or walking,
they single-mindedly and exclusively contemplate the words and letters of the Lotus Sutra.
To practice diligence without lying down, as if one's head were on fire—
this is called the practice of the characteristics of words.
Such a practitioner disregards both body and life.
If one’s practice is perfected, one will immediately see Samantabhadra, whose body is the color of vajra, riding upon the six-tusked elephant king and standing before that person.
He will then brandish a vajra toward the practitioner’s eyes.
The offenses that obstruct the Path are extinguished;
the faculty of the eye becomes pure, and one is able to see Śākyamuni as well as the seven Buddhas.
Furthermore, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
and with a sincere heart repents,
prostrating oneself fully before all these Buddhas.

second, the flesh eye and the divine eye; and third, the wisdom of the bodhisattva path.
Second is the hundred-thousand-myriad-billions *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*,
by which one fulfills the bodhisattva’s wisdom of the lineage of the path and attains the purity of the dharma-eye.
Third is the *dhāraṇī* of skillful means in the sound of the Dharma.
Being fully endowed with the bodhisattva’s wisdom of all modes and the pure Buddha-eye,

or else, one may attain this perfection through cultivation in a single lifetime.
Or it may be attained in two lifetimes;
at the very slowest, one attains it in three lifetimes.
However, if one clings to body and life or craves the four types of offerings, one will be unable to practice diligently.
Even after passing through kalpas, one does not attain it;

What is meant by "peace"? It is called peace because the mind is unmoving amidst all phenomena. What is meant by "bliss"?
It is called bliss because there is no aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) amidst all phenomena. What is meant by "practice"?
It is called practice because it benefits both oneself and others.
The answer is:
"All phenomena" refers to the three poisons, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen constituents, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
These are called all dharmas.
Within all these dharmas, a bodhisattva employs the wisdom of the three kinds of patience.
The first is called patience toward sentient beings.
The second is called the patience of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-kṣānti*).

The third is called the patience of the supernatural powers of the ocean of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-samudra-abhijñā-kṣānti*). [The fourth is] the patience regarding sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*).
That which is called "patience regarding arising" is termed "Dharma-nature patience.
That which is called "patience regarding the ocean of the Dharma-realm's supernormal powers" is termed "Great Patience."
The first two types of patience are called the patience that destroys ignorance and afflictions,
and are also termed the patience of noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).
They are called "noble practice" because they are the sphere of activity for noble ones.
When an ordinary person is able to practice this, they immediately enter the stage of the noble ones;
this is called the noble practice.
As for "great patience":
Possessing the five supernatural powers as well as the sixth,
and fully endowed with the four bases of psychic power,
he stood before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the various heavenly kings.
Facing all discourse, being able to awaken to everything— both mundane and transcendent— in a single thought-moment is called Great Patience (*mahākṣānti*).
Having a mind that is unmoved amidst all supernormal powers and being fully endowed with the noble path is called Noble Patience (*āryakṣānti*).
The three kinds of patience are precisely the practice of peaceful dwelling through right wisdom free from attachment. Question:
What is called "patience toward birth"? Why is it also called "patience toward sentient beings"?
What is called "immovable patience"?
It is further named "Peace.
The answer is:
the patience toward sentient beings (kṣānti) is called the cause.
The patience of sentient beings is called the fruit;
the cause is the cause of sentient beings,
and the fruit is the fruit of sentient beings.
The cause is ignorance;
the effect is bodily formations.
By observing the cause with right wisdom, one destroys ignorance and cuts off all afflictions.
All phenomena are ultimately without conjunction;
they have no characteristic of aggregation, nor is any disintegration perceived.
When a bodhisattva, through subtle wisdom, understands this Noble Truth of Origination, it is called the patience of birth.
If there is no combination, there is neither movement nor flow, and thus no arising.
The patience of sentient beings is called the bodily engagement in various sensations;
sensation is suffering.
There are three types of feeling:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neutral feeling.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Why is this? Because when one is beaten or reviled, one contemplates painful sensation.
Being struck is physical suffering;
being reviled is mental suffering.
Food, drink, clothing, fine textures, and offerings are called physical pleasure.
Furthermore, various forms of physical contact are also called bodily pleasure;
praising and extolling [the recipient] is called mental pleasure.
Thus, one ultimately obtains excellent gifts.
The eye sees what has not yet been felt;
once it has been felt, it is also called mental pleasure.
One contemplates this ignorance-feeling, as well as suffering and pleasure.
When experiencing suffering,
give rise to patience and compassion and do not harbor anger;
when experiencing pleasure...
Contemplating the mind detached from feeling, one does not become greedily attached;
when experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
one remains far removed from equanimity and does not give rise to ignorance.
All sensations are ultimately empty, quiescent, and devoid of arising or ceasing;
therefore, these three types of sensation all arise from the deluded mind of a single thought-moment.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva contemplates these offerings, beatings, praises, or insults, [he perceives them as such].
The giver and the receiver are like a dream or a magical illusion.
Who strikes? Who reviles? Who receives? Who rejoices? Who is angry?
Both the giver and the receiver are merely false conceptions.
Contemplate these deluded thoughts:
ultimately there is no mind, no self, and no person.
The six parts—the male and female forms, enemies, relatives, neutral persons, heads, and so forth—are like reflections in space; because they are ungraspable, they do not exist.
This is called "immovability.
As it is said in the *Sui-zhuyi Samādhi* (Samādhi of Following One's Own Intent):
"The Bodhisattva, within the eighteen realms (*dhātus*), has no mind of arising or ceasing."
He also teaches sentient beings that there is neither arising nor ceasing;
from the beginning of birth and death until the ultimate attainment of bodhi,
the nature of all phenomena is ultimately immovable.
That is to say: the nature of the eye, the nature of form, and the nature of consciousness;
the natures of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
and even the natures of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
The nature of all sensations produced through the conditions of ear-consciousness;
the nature of all sensations produced through the conditions of nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness;
are without self and without other, because they are ultimately empty.
This is called immovability.
Because one awakens oneself and awakens others, it is termed peace.
One personally severs the three sensations so that they do not arise.
Because ultimate emptiness and quiescence are devoid of the three types of sensation,
no sensations whatsoever ultimately arise;
this is called bliss.
Within all dharmas, the mind has no place to move;
likewise, one teaches sentient beings that within all dharmas,
the mind has nothing upon which to move.
To practice meditation without ceasing and to uphold the Lotus Sutra together is what is called "practice."
This is as explained in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* regarding the meaning of the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya-āyatana*),
and also as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and the Tathāgata-garbha.
The meanings of the "Peaceful Practice" (*sukhavihāra*) are numerous and not limited to one.
To speak briefly once more:
within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of all ordinary beings,
ignorance, craving, and attachment give rise to sensation, mindfulness, and clinging.
Purely committing sinful austerities cannot bring peace to oneself;
as birth and death are not severed,
there is therefore no joy.
This is called ascetic practice.
Among the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, all practitioners of the two vehicles—the śrāvakas—apply the contemplation of antidotes;
through the method of the contemplation of impurity, they are able to sever lustful desire.
The practice of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever hatred;
the practice of the contemplation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) can sever delusion.
When explained by their distinct names, these are called the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
These four foundations of mindfulness have thirty-seven distinct names known as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
One contemplates the impurity of the body and is able to understand that this impure body is the root of ignorance, empty and without a place of arising.
The method of the contemplation on impurity can destroy the view of a self-body, male-female distinctions, and hatred or love;
even those who stand between these states all return to emptiness and stillness.
This is called destroying the demon of afflictions.
Contemplating the eighteen elements and the three types of feeling, one observes the external aggregate of painful feeling and the internal aggregate of painful feeling.
One knows that this aggregate of painful feeling—everything within the range of the body and mind, where feelings are experienced and clung to—is entirely suffering.
One relinquishes them without clinging to internal pleasant feelings,
external pleasant feelings,
or both internal and external pleasant feelings.
Contemplate this pleasant feeling:
because the mind is greedily attached to it, it can act as a cause of suffering.
Abandoning it and not receiving it, one knows that all pleasant feelings are entirely empty.
The two contemplations of suffering and pleasure can destroy conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When the mind abides in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one first abandons both suffering and pleasure,
thereby attaining neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*).
Because of this attachment,
it is further ignorance.
One then further contemplates this sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant.
It is without dependence and is impermanent and subject to decay. Why is this?
Because by abandoning suffering and pleasure, one attains neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Since the two observations of suffering and pleasure have neither place of arising nor place of cessation,
being ultimately empty and quiescent, from where could that which is neither painful nor pleasant arise?
When observing in this way:
Emptiness is without anything to be attained and without anything to be relinquished.
Since there is nothing to be relinquished, one likewise does not attain the dharma of "nothing to be relinquished.
If there were no conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there would be no ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
When both the true and the false are stilled,
one then destroys the demons of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
One contemplates that the mind is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and does not abide.
One observes from what this mind originally arises.
When observing in this way,
one does not perceive the mind at all, nor its arising or ceasing.
Neither annihilated nor eternal, one does not abide in the middle way;
having contemplated thus, there is no death-māra.
Within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates all phenomena.
Whether they be wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena,
or indeterminate phenomena.
All are like space and cannot be selected;
within all phenomena, the mind is ultimately unmoving.
Without even abiding in the mark of movement, one attains the Samādhi of Immovability.
Furthermore, there are devas who, by abandoning the three types of sensation, attain this liberation;
it is called the practice of suffering and pleasure.
Both cause and effect are termed the path of the śrāvaka, not the path of the bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas of dull faculties also differ from them in this contemplation regarding non-acceptance and non-rejection. Why is this?
Because form, mind, and the three types of sensation ultimately do not arise.
Because the eighteen elements do not exist,
there is no internal or external grasping of sensation.
Since there is no sensation, there is nothing to be relinquished.
Although the practice of contemplation is the same, because it is uninterrupted by the three types of sensation, skillful wisdom and expedient means can be fully perfected;
therefore, this is called the "Practice of Peaceful Living.
Within the Practice of Peaceful Living, contemplation does not proceed in this manner.
"Being straightforward, he set aside expedient means and taught only the unsurpassed path.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
"How will these bodhisattvas be able to preach this sutra in the evil world of the future?
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to expound this sutra in the future evil age,
they should abide securely in four dharmas.
First, by abiding in the sphere of conduct and the sphere of association of a bodhisattva,
one is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
What is meant by the "sphere of conduct" of a bodhisattva?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the stage of patience,
being gentle, compliant, and harmonious without being abrupt or violent,
their mind remains undisturbed.
Furthermore, while not engaging with any phenomena, one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are;
neither engaging nor discriminating—
this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is meant by "abiding on the ground of patience"?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of patience:
first, patience toward sentient beings.
Second is the patience regarding phenomena (dharma-kṣānti);
third is the great patience,
which is also called the patience of supernormal powers (abhijñā-kṣānti).
Regarding the patience of sentient beings, there are three types of intention.
As for the first intention:
when a bodhisattva receives beating, verbal abuse, humiliation, disparagement, or slander from others.
At that time, one should practice patience and not retaliate.
One should reflect in this way:
"It is because I have a body that they come to strike and revile me."
It is like a bow that must first be drawn before the arrow hits its mark.
If I were without a body, who would come to strike?
I shall now diligently cultivate the contemplation of emptiness.
If the contemplation of emptiness is perfected, there is no one who can strike or kill me.
When being reviled, one should contemplate with right mindfulness.
Yet these sounds of abuse arise and perish as soon as they are uttered;
they do not coexist before and after.
When examined with careful scrutiny, they are likewise without arising or ceasing, like an echo in space.
Who insults and who receives the insult?
Sound does not come to enter the ear,
nor does the ear go out to grasp the sound.
Having contemplated in this way, there is no longer any anger or joy.
Regarding these two mental states:
the bodhisattva never strikes or reviles any sentient being whatsoever.
He always uses gentle speech to protect the other's feelings,
desiring to guide them;
even when subjected to beating or verbal abuse, his mind remains steadfast and undisturbed.
This is called the patience of sentient beings.
When sentient beings see the patience of a bodhisattva, they immediately give rise to the mind of enlightenment for the sake of all beings.
Therefore, it is called "patience toward sentient beings.
As for the third intention:
it is for the sake of subduing sentient beings who are stubborn and evil.
To cause them to reform their minds,
he may sometimes use harsh words to disparage or revile them,
so that they may feel shame and give rise to a wholesome mind.
This is called the patience of sentient beings.
What is meant by "humiliation"?
That which one cannot endure is precisely what is called humiliation.
There is no other separate dharma.
It is asked:
To not feel anger when struck or reviled, and to respond with compassion and gentle speech—can this be called patience?
When Bodhisattvas encounter sentient beings who are fierce and evil, they are unable to endure them;
appearing as if harboring thoughts of anger, they strike, beat,
and revile them in order to subdue these wicked people.
If one causes that person to suffer,
how can it still be called patience?
The answer is:
Not retaliating when struck or reviled—
this is the patience regarding external deportment within the mundane precepts;
furthermore, by contemplating that internal emptiness, sounds and so forth are empty, and the body and mind are tranquil and still, one does not give rise to resentment or hatred.
This refers to a newly initiated bodhisattva who practices the skillful means of precepts,
concentration, wisdom, and patience merely to quell worldly criticism;
they are not a great bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas, seeing only those places where sentient beings may be benefited,
immediately tame them for the sake of protecting the Mahāyāna and safeguarding the True Dharma.
It is not necessary for all [teachings] to be compassionate and gentle in speech;
this is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
For example, in the past, King Śibi protected the Vaipulya sūtras.
By causing five hundred brahmins to end their lives and enter the Avīci Hell, he caused them to give rise to the bodhicitta;
is this not indeed great loving-kindness and great compassion?
This is precisely the Great Patience.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of a king of the country of Aryadeśa who protected the Dharma Master Bodhivṛddhi and,
by extension, protected the True Dharma.
By killing one person— a breaker of precepts and an evil man within the kingdom—
he enabled the Dharma Master Juede to practice the True Dharma.
After the king’s life ended, he was immediately reborn before the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern quarter.
They shall become the foremost great disciples.
Their ministers and military retinues shall also be born before the Buddha Akṣobhya as the second and third disciples.
All those people of black and white evil who have broken the precepts will,
at the end of their lives, fall into the Avīci Hell;
within that hell, they will recognize their own original transgressions.
He thought to himself:
"I have harmed the Dharma Master Jue;
the king will kill me."
Thereupon, each gave rise to the thought [of awakening] and developed the bodhicitta;
they emerged from hell and were reborn in the presence of King Bodhivardhana and King Sudeva.
Acting as a disciple to seek the unsurpassed path—
this is the great skillful means and patience of a bodhisattva,
which is not something that can be accomplished by a minor bodhisattva.
How can it be said that he was not patient?
The Dharma Master Jue-de was Kāśyapa Buddha;
the King You-de was Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla should also be like this.
Why, then, would it not be called "Great Forbearance"?
If there is a bodhisattva who practices mundane forbearance...
If one does not discipline evil persons,
allowing them to perpetuate their evil and destroy the True Dharma,
such a bodhisattva is actually an evil Māra and not a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, they cannot be called śrāvakas.
Why is this? Because they seek mundane patience and are thus unable to protect the Dharma.
Although outwardly appearing to practice patience while purely engaging in demonic activities,
if a bodhisattva cultivates great loving-kindness and great compassion,
they will be fully endowed with forbearance, establish the Mahāyāna, and protect sentient beings.
One must not cling exclusively to worldly patience.
Why is this? If there is a bodhisattva who seeks to protect wicked people, [he should do so with wisdom].
Unable to be disciplined or punished,
they cause evil to flourish and afflict virtuous people,
thereby destroying the True Dharma.
This person is truly not one who merely puts on a false appearance;
they constantly say:
"I practice patience."
When that person’s life ends, they fall into hell together with those evil people.
For this reason, it cannot be called "patience.
What, then, is meant by "dwelling on the ground of patience"?
The bodhisattva’s patience can give rise to all the meritorious qualities of the Buddha-way.
Just as the great earth produces and nurtures all the myriad things of the world, so too is patience.
The Bodhisattva practices the dharma of great patience;
at times he practices loving-kindness, compassion, and gentle speech,
not retaliating when struck or reviled.
Or again, they may engage in harsh speech and abusive words,
beating and striking sentient beings,
even unto the end of their lives.
Both of these types of patience are for the purpose of protecting the True Dharma and taming sentient beings;
they are not something that can be accomplished by beginners.
This is called being one who possesses the patience of the dharma of patience.
There are three kinds of intentions.
The first intention is to personally cultivate noble conduct.
One contemplates that all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent—
neither arising nor ceasing, and neither annihilated nor eternal.
This is called contemplating the emptiness of the eye-faculty within all phenomena.
The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty.
The eye and forms are empty;
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are all empty.
Contemplate that eye-consciousness is empty, and that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are empty.
There is no self, no person, no sentient being, no creator, no doer, and no experiencer.
The retribution for good and evil is like flowers in the sky.
All the great aggregates, elements, and sense bases are empty;
the three, six, and eighteen have no names or designations;
they have no beginning, no end, and no middle.
Its nature is fundamentally and eternally tranquil;
the mind does not stir amidst any phenomena.
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the patience of dharmas.
The second meaning is that the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and likewise teaches this Dharma to sentient beings.
Observing the distinctions among those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties,
he employs skillful means to lead them to abide in the Mahāyāna,
progressing from the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha to that of Bodhisattva.
The three types of contemplative practice are unified as one;
there is no distinction between the holy practices of form and mind.
From the very beginning, the two vehicles and ordinary beings, as well as the sages, have been thus.
The single dharmakāya is itself the Buddha.
As for the third intention:
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates sentient beings with sovereign wisdom.
They tame them through the skillful means of sympathetic cooperation (*sāṃvṛtya-samānārthatā*):
sometimes manifesting the practice of precepts and subtle conduct,
and sometimes manifesting the breaking of precepts and a lack of dignified decorum.
In order to fulfill their original vows,
they manifest bodies within the six realms of existence to discipline sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the skillful means of practicing the patience of dharmas to transform sentient beings.
The great patience is called the patience of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-kṣānti*).
What is meant by the patience of supernormal powers?
When a bodhisattva first initially resolves his mind [on enlightenment]...
I vow to deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and diligently cultivate the Dharma of the six perfections: generosity,
ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The factors of the path of the three vehicles,
all-encompassing wisdom,
and the realization of nirvana.
He enters deeply into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Looking upward, he does not see the Buddhas; looking downward, he does not see sentient beings.
Then he forms this thought:
"I originally vowed to deliver all sentient beings.
Now, I do not see any sentient beings at all.
Will this not be a violation of my former vow?"
At the moment of forming this thought,
all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions immediately manifested their physical bodies.
They praised this bodhisattva with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O great son of noble family!"
"Recall your original vows and do not abandon sentient beings.
When we Buddhas first began our study of the Way,
we made great vows to extensively deliver all sentient beings."
Having diligently studied the Way and realized nirvana,
he entered deeply into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and no longer perceived sentient beings. Yet,
recollecting his original vows, he immediately gave rise to a sense of regret and turned his attention back toward sentient beings.
At that moment, one sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions praising in unison:
"We, too, like you, remember our original vows;
do not abandon sentient beings."
When the Buddhas of the ten directions spoke these words,
the Bodhisattvas, hearing the speech of the Buddhas at that time,
felt great joy in their hearts and immediately attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Seated in the midst of empty space, they see all Buddhas of the ten directions;
they are fully endowed with the wisdom of all Buddhas,
and in a single thought-moment, they completely know the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He also knows the mental activities of all sentient beings;
in a single thought-moment, he is able to observe them all universally,
desiring at once to deliver all sentient beings.
Because the mind is vast, it is called "Great Patience.
Because it is fully endowed with the qualities of the Buddhas and Great Beings,
it is named "Great Patience."
In order to deliver sentient beings,
the physical body and wisdom manifest in various forms according to the capacities of those to be taught;
within a single thought-moment, all bodies are manifested.
To preach the Dharma at one time with a single voice that can produce the sound of no-sound,
whereby immeasurable sentient beings simultaneously attain the Way—
this is called the patience of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-kṣānti*).
Regarding "gentle, kind, and compliant":
first, one personally tames and subdues one's own mind;
second, one gently subdues sentient beings.
Harmony refers to practicing the six points of harmonious respect, maintaining the precepts, cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom, and realizing the dharma of liberation.
It extends even to the taming of sentient beings' anger through patience, and regarding both those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, all are identical in their nature to *nirvāṇa*.
What are called the six harmonies are:
harmony of mind, harmony of body, harmony of speech, harmony of precepts, harmony of benefit, and harmony of view.
These are what is meant by "skillful compliance."

Skillfully knowing the dispositions of the faculties of sentient beings and taming them accordingly is called "common purpose" (samānārthatā), which is comprised within the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
Gentleness is termed "dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti).
One who is skillfully compliant is said to possess great patience;
such a person does not act with sudden violence when studying the Buddha-dharma.
He is not hurried or impetuous.
His attainment of realization, his external conduct, his dignified demeanor,
and his transformation of sentient beings are likewise so.
Regarding "the mind is not startled":
to be startled is called agitation.
To be sudden, violent, and hurried is precisely what constitutes being startled and agitated.
Whether it be pleasant sounds or foul sounds,
even thunderclaps, or any evil objects as well as virtuous forms—
when heard by the ear or seen by the eye, the mind remains entirely unmoved.
Because they understand the dharma of emptiness and are ultimately without mind,
it is said that they are not startled.
Furthermore, regarding the non-practice of dharmas:
within the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, all afflictive dharmas are ultimately empty;
therefore, they are without mind and without locus.
Furthermore, within the dharmas of dhyāna and liberation, there is no wisdom, no mind, and no activity;
yet one contemplates all dharmas according to their true nature:
the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
All are the true nature of suchness;
they have no beginning or end, no arising or ceasing,
no affliction and no liberation.
Furthermore, those who neither practice nor discriminate perceive that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are neither one nor different;
ordinary beings and Buddhas are non-dual within the single dharma-realm.
Therefore, it cannot be differentiated.
Furthermore, because non-duality is not perceived, one speaks of "non-practice" and "non-differentiation.
The characteristic of non-differentiation is itself unattainable.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi of namelessness,
although there is no place of dwelling, they are able to manifest all supernatural powers without relying on expedient means.
This is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Upon first entering the stage of the sages, one is immediately equal [to them].
This is the immovable, true, and eternal *dharmakāya*, not the *dharmakāya* of expedient means or conditioned conformity.
It may also be called the realization of the *tathāgatagarbha*, even unto the *manogarbha*.
